extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in NLP / affective computing working on multimodal sarcasm and humor detection in code-mixed conversational settings
extracted.subtask_description: Detect and classify each utterance in a multi-speaker conversational dialog as sarcastic/non-sarcastic and humorous/non-humorous, using multi-modal inputs (text, acoustic, optionally visual) and dialog context; applied to Hindi-English code-mixed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task formulation (utterance-level binary classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a sequence of utterances U = (u1, u2, ..., un) in a dialog video, classify each utterance into – (i) sarcastic or non-sarcastic, and (ii) humorous or non-humorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each utterance ui may have multiple modality representations (textual uT_i, acoustic uA_i, visual uV_i). Classification is performed per utterance within the dialog context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sarcasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarcasm is defined as an expression meant to criticize, taunt, or hurt someone’s feeling in a sober and explicitly non-disrespectful manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all sarcastic statements are amusing; annotation should follow this conceptual definition when assigning sarcastic labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous statements aim to incite amusing or comic feelings with the intention to make their audience laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A light-hearted sarcastic statement which does not offend can be interpreted as humorous; annotate humor separately from sarcasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotate both sarcasm and humor per utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: For each utterance, assign appropriate sarcasm (sarcastic or non-sarcastic) and humor (humorous or non-humorous) labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the two labels independently — an utterance can be sarcastic and/or humorous. Use majority voting across annotators to aggregate labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation protocol and inter-annotator agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple annotators (three used here) and aggregate labels by majority voting. Report inter-rater agreement (Cohen Kappa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper reports Cohen Kappa = 0.654 (humor) and 0.681 (sarcasm); include such agreement statistics to validate annotation quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset composition (dialog-level, multi-party)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect multi-party conversational dialogs (MaSaC: ~1,200 multi-party dialogs from TV show 'Sarabhai vs. Sarabhai'), split by scenes into dialogs, and split dialogs into utterances (~15,000 utterances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each dialog is treated as a standalone conversation; context for an utterance is restricted to the current dialog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modalities to include and noise considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage distinct and diverse information offered by each modality while reducing the effect of noise among multi-modal information sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a modality (e.g., visual frames) contains irrelevant content or noise (multiple actors, low-quality frames) it may be better to exclude it as it can 'defile the learning process by attending to irrelevant content.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality selection for this work
rubrics_metrics.description: Use textual and acoustic modalities for modeling; visual modality was excluded in main models due to noisy / low-quality frames and presence of multiple actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual features were extracted experimentally (Affectiva, GoogleNet) but yielded poor results; include visual only if frame quality and actor alignment support useful signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of multi-modal signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark boundaries of each utterance on the time spectrum by detecting prolonged silence, discard silence, and map corresponding speech and visual frames to utterances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate alignment is necessary to extract utterance-level acoustic and visual features that correspond to the transcripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter removal from audio
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove audience laughter and background noise from audio to avoid the model overfitting on audience reactions when the target task is humor classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper uses Audacity's laughter suppression approach (identify laughter frequency bands, suppress above threshold, smooth sample). Document and justify any audio cleaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic speech recognition for transcripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an ASR system (Gnani.ai, Google Speech API-based) to extract speech transcripts for each utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify ASR quality especially for romanized code-mixed Hindi-English; manual correction may be necessary if ASR fails on transliterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual feature representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pre-trained FastText multilingual word embeddings (300-dimensional, uncased) for tokens; achieved >90% coverage of vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multilingual embeddings help handle code-mixing; document embedding coverage and consider alternatives (BERT, multilingual BERT) as baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic feature representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract MFCC-based acoustic features (up to 128 MFCCs per frame) using Librosa and obtain utterance-level representations by applying a time-distributed 1D convolution over MFCC frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acoustic features capture pitch, intensity and prosodic cues that complement textual semantics for sarcasm/humor detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual feature representation (experimental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual features were extracted using Affectiva API and GoogleNet (Va, Vg) for evaluation but performed poorly due to low-quality frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If visual signals are high-quality and actor-specific, include; otherwise exclude to prevent noisy attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utterance-level hierarchical localized attention (H-ATNU)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute efficient textual utterance representation using a hierarchy of localized attentions that attend to a small portion of the input sentence at a time; AtnWidthU controls window size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AtnWidthU in [2,5] was tested and AtnWidthU = 3 was optimal in experiments. Hierarchical attention supports extraction of long-term relations by progressively attending to wider spans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialog-level modality-specific contextual attention (C-ATND)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ separate dialog-level attention modules that compute attention weights α (acoustic), β (textual), and γ (cross-modal) over preceding utterances to capture contextual importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AtnWidthD (number of preceding utterances considered) was best at 5; attention weights signify the importance of contextual utterances for classifying the current utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtering / gating mechanism to reduce inter-modal noise
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a gating/filtering mechanism that learns interactions among modalities and filters noise via sigmoid gates (σ) and tanh activations to control information flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gating values near 0 block irrelevant information; near 1 allow forwarding. Filtering improved bi-modal/tri-modal performance in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual skip connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use residual skip connections when forming final attended representations to stabilize learning (e.g., concatenating attended context with original hidden representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Residual connections were used to form the final attended representations ˆh^A_i, ˆh^T_i, ˆh^{AT}_i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence modeling and LSTM configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: Model dialog-level sequences using LSTM(s); in experiments forward LSTM with 128-dimensional hidden state per modality was used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modality-specific LSTMs to learn sequences of hidden states h^T_i and h^A_i before applying contextual attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training hyperparameters and optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dropout = 40%, batch size = 32, ReLU activation, output sigmoid with binary cross-entropy loss, and Adam optimizer for training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document hyperparameters and justify choices; these were the settings used for reported experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics and preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute precision, recall, F1-score, and accuracy for both sarcasm and humor classification; prefer F1-score due to unbalanced label distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both accuracy and F1 for completeness but emphasize F1 when classes are imbalanced (e.g., sarcastic/non-sarcastic: 391/1185).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental comparisons / baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate multiple variants: uni-modal (textual/acoustic/visual), hierarchical vs. mean/BERT utterance embeddings, with/without dialog-level attention, with/without filtering, and multi-modal fusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to strong baselines (e.g., TBERT, Tavg, LSTM variants) and report per-modality and combined results to quantify contribution of each component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention-context window selection guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The contextual window size for dialog-level attention (AtnWidthD) should capture nearby context but not too far; in experiments performance degraded beyond 5 preceding utterances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose AtnWidthD to reflect the empirically observed proximity of sarcasm/humor context (~5 utterances). Too small a window lacks context; too large introduces irrelevant signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset split and validation protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Split dialogs into train/test sets (paper: 1,100 train dialogs and 90 test dialogs) and use 10% of train as validation. Report counts of utterances and class distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain dialog-level split (no leak across train/test) and report speaker-wise distributions and label counts to show dataset characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle code-mixing and language identification challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Code-mixed inputs require word-level language identification and multilingual/cross-lingual representations; transliteration ambiguity (e.g., 'main') complicates dictionary lookups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multilingual embeddings, consider language identification preprocessing, and analyze model performance against degree of code-mixing. Paper observed better performance on utterances with more English words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretability via attention heatmaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Use attention heatmaps (textual, acoustic, cross-modal) to analyze which contextual utterances the model attends to and to justify model decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heatmaps should show higher attention weights for contextually relevant utterances; use them to validate model behavior qualitatively.
